newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: Puerto Rico Gov says unemployment down in Dec.
newsitem.headline: Puerto Rico Gov says unemployment down in Dec.

text.p: Puerto Rico Gov. Pedro Rossello said in a speech Monday night that Puerto Rico's unemployment rate in December was 10.1 percent, its lowest rate in 25 years, an indicator that he said reflects the island's robust economy.
He also said during the first State of the Commonwealth address of his second term that tourism was flourishing, with a 35 percent increase in hotel registrations from 1992 to 1996.
"These results give us a clear plan of action, a similar path, but more proactive, for our next for years of work," he said, announcing a series of economic proposals.

Rossello said he would submit a series of reforms to the legislature to cut taxes for individuals and businesses. One of the most important would give private companies a 10 percent standard reduction on capital gains from the current 20 percent if they convert to public companies before 2000.

And he proposed increasing deductions for individual retirement accounts by $500 to $3,000, as well as adding a $200 tax deductions for families who pay for child care and a $1,000 deduction for people aged 16 to 25 who work. He also said he would seek to allow taxpayers to use 50 percent of their IRAs for investment in local companies.

To foster a local corporate debt market, Rossello proposed dropping tax rates from their current 36 to 39 percent range to 17 percent. The new local market would overcome the loss last year of Section 936, a federal tax break that had been given to U.S. companies that invest in Puerto Rico. Some U.S. firms, having lost the tax break on interest, have withdrawn millions from the commonwealth's financial system.

Rossello said he would extend his current government health card plan to 12 more municipalities, which would mean that 73 of Puerto Rico's 78 municipalities would be included in his health care reform by July 1999.

He also said he would seek to establish a new family benefits card to be introduced this year. The card would be similar to an automated teller machine card, where holders would be able to use it to tap into government aid including nutritional assistance to women and children.

Rossello pledged to bring violent crime down to 50 percent of its 1992 rate, and said he would push for work programs to reduce the number of people relying on government assistance. And he pledged to establish a commission led by Secretary of State Norma Burgos to cut down on government bureaucracy.
Rossello had told reporters before his speech that he would inform the Legislature next month, when he presents his fiscal 1998 budget, how much the new incentives would cost the government.
